Cal did not laugh. Cal put down a mug and put a hand on a blank bit of wall by a broad doorway. "This is your spot. Think about what fits. Talk to folks who visit our hall."

Boris put his king back in its roll. Cal had said small, and his crown was almost as broad as his full wall. Now this job was shrinking in all wrong ways.

Boris did art for fun. His top work was a painting of a bowl, drawn at his flat, with nobody watching. His worst was a portrait of his dad, which his aunt said had caught his curtains. A hall mural would stay in public. Folks could scorn it without putting it away.

At his flat, Boris built a small trial board. Onto it, Boris put a light ground coat and swaths of brown, pink, and gold. His pad had a drying log. A jar for his brush stood apart from a jar with a RINSING tag. His kit had surplus rags, scraps of card, and a flat brush for broad swaths. His small acts of planning brought comfort following a vast gap in his facts.

On Thursday morning Uma was washing mugs at our hall. Uma had known it from childhood to now. Boris sought an important day for his mural.

"Soup," Uma said.

Boris sat still, waiting.

"Our usual lunch. Long ago, prior to this mug stock, all our cups had grips so small nobody could hold a cup firmly. I would put a bit of cloth round a grip. My husband said it was washing hung up to dry."

"Was a particular lunch outstanding?"

"Most did not vary much. That was why I sought it out. You could count on lunch and company."

Uma took a mug from its drying rack and put both hands round it. Uma's hands had brown spots and a strong thumb. Boris caught that thumb in charcoal in his pad. His plan was a grand occasion. Now a drawing of how to hold a cup was growing in its spot.

"I cannot paint so much soup," Boris said.

"No. You can paint our lunch spot: a broad plank on four stout posts."

Uma got back to washing. Boris did a quick drawing of a chair's curving back against a long board. That arc had a charm his king's crown did not, though Boris was not willing to admit it.

Sal brought back a folding chair that day, following lunch. Boris sought a story Sal would wish to hold onto.

Sal shot a look past him to a cupboard. "My first class."

"What class?"

"Word study. I was forty. I could count sacks at work. I did not know how to turn script into words on my son's school slip. I would walk to this hall on Thursdays."

Boris almost put Sal with a book in his pad, but caught his own hand. "What was in your thoughts as you sat?"

"Our floor. For a half hour. I thought all would know why I was in that spot. Our tutor finally put an inquiry to us: which word was important to us? I said Tom, my son."

Sal was not smiling. Boris put his pad down.

"You can skip my portrait," Sal said. "It was no grand show of skill. I struck out my writing. Our tutor did too. That was a comfort."

Boris put forward a scrap of writing to stand for that class. Sal said it could work, if it was plainly a work in motion. A row of script without a flaw would imply a wrong story.

That night Boris brought his king out of its roll and saw a blank, placid crowd. No thumb, no floor to look at, no son. That crowd had only a task of making its king look tall. Boris put his drawing flat on his floor by his trial board and took up an additional bit of card.

On Friday Linn was at our hall to count chairs for a Saturday ball. Linn took a long walk across it, counting aloud. Boris sought Linn's first account of a ball in that hall.

"It was awful," Linn said. "I took a boy with boots too big for him. My boots had too tight a fit. Both of us sat by a door for half our night."

Boris had thought this account would glow with joy. "Did you marry him?"

"No. I took off for my flat. On my following visit I had no companion and had much fun."

Linn put a hand on our doorway. Folks sat by it to catch a bit of calm in a ball, possibly worn out, possibly waiting for a bold mood. A painting of nothing but whirling pairs would skip all such folks.

"Put in a pair of boots," Linn said. "And room for a soul who has not stood up to join in."

Boris put boots down by a chair in his pad. No portraits of Linn and that boy. His pad had a host of folks now; Boris did not want a full account to shrink into a portrait of who had told it.

His following draft put 3 things around a long board: a mug in two hands, a partly drawn row of script, and a chair with boots down by it. Across from this, a doorway stood ajar against plain light. No king. Boris was fond of that light most of all. It was not drawn from a particular story, but could put all 3 in a spot with room to grow.

Cal brought Uma in to look at this draft prior to painting. Uma took a long, calm look.

"That is a good board," Uma said. "But who can sit at it?"

Boris did not grasp that criticism.

Uma put a hand on his chairs. All stood in a firm ring round that board. Boots sat down by a chair put right up to its rim. No vacant spot for anybody to sit down.

Boris had a sharp wish to say this was art, not a floor plan. Nothing got said until that wish had lost its grip. Finally Boris took out his charcoal.

"If I pull this chair out?"

"That would do much good."

"And shift that script toward this spot?"

Uma was nodding. Uma also sought a big pot in that board's midpoint. Boris did a trial on scrap, but that pot hid his partly drawn script. Boris told Uma why no pot would go in. Uma put both palms up. "It is your painting. I was thinking about lunch."

That did him good. Criticism could modify an option without taking all options away. Boris put a gap round his chair, but his pot did not go in. His light still had its spot. In this final draft, you could join that board without a tight squash among all its symbols.

Boris put Saturday morning into marking his main forms on that wall. His wall's spans and his draft had matching grids. Cal had our door ajar whilst Boris brought his kit in, but took off to a job of his own. Boris did his art solo, with a radio too soft to catch its words.

Boris put his doorway in first. Its light was warm gold, distinct from a blank wall. His long board and its broad arc took form following that. His trial board could confirm how brown would look against gold prior to putting both on his mural. His hands took most of his day. A thumb could look just as fat as a hot dog if Boris did it too fast.

On Sunday his arm caught that brown jar. A thin run of paint slid down his light doorway, right through that gap Boris had fought to hold vacant. Boris stood watching it, clinging to a foolish thought that it might stop of its own accord.

It did not.

Boris sought to scrub that full patch. His trial board lay by his boots. On it, a trial drip had grown broad following a rub whilst paint was still fluid. Boris took a dry rag, caught paint still running down, and did nothing to that blot for now. Boris put a scrap of card atop that jar and put it past his kit, out of his arm's path. First, stop causing an additional fault.

As his patch got dry, Boris put paint on his boots in that mural. Boris had a roll for lunch and took a look at his paint log. Following a trial on his board, Boris put a light ground coat back on that spoilt strip. It took two slow coats and an additional wait. His doorway had lost a bit of its span. Boris took a matching bit off its far rim, so both rims had an inward shift. A narrow doorway now fit his plan.

His light still had its spot in this mural. This mishap had not brought magic charm to his art. His planning had only shown him how to go on without causing additional harm.

By lunch on Monday, this mural was dry. Sal was first to stand by that partly drawn script. Boris had put only a handful of marks in, nothing anybody could truly say aloud. A faint crossing-out was still plain down by its last mark.

"That looks about right," Sal said. "Not so tidy I would think you won a diploma."

Cal brought a small sign saying BORIS. A man by our door sought to know why no king was in sight. That man was fond of royal art. An additional visitor said his hands had too much bulk. A child said his boots should look muddy.

Boris could put forward an account for all such complaints. Only his king got an account: his king was his own fiction, without a supporting fact. Boris was doubtful about his hands. Both might look too big. Boris could look again in a month.

At lunch Boris sat at our actual board, with mugs that did not match and soup that was a bit thin. Nobody put a full lunch hour into discussing his mural. Sal put an inquiry to Linn about Saturday. Uma found an additional spoon. Cal had our door ajar for a visitor with a bag.

Boris cast a look from his mural's doorway to our actual door. His art had room for anybody to walk in. Our hall was using that room without calling on him for an account of it. Boris had his soup, did his mug's washing-up, and put his old king drawing in a box of drafts, intact. It could show him how much a man might wrongly think prior to putting a small inquiry to anybody.

prompt: Write a connected practical guide for four fictional students completing a class project over three weeks. They must produce a poster and a six-minute oral presentation about an assigned topic; the teacher has supplied a rubric and source list. Explain how to read the brief, divide work fairly, keep a shared record, check claims against the supplied sources, combine different writing styles, rehearse transitions, and submit on time. Include a concrete three-week plan, a six-minute speaking allocation that adds up, a sample work record, and respectful wording for addressing a missed commitment. Cover how to handle a disputed claim, unequal confidence in speaking, and one member being absent on presentation day. Do not invent the assigned topic or official grading rules. Write 2,048 to 2,560 Qwen tokens of substantive useful advice.
response:
Four pupils, Ali, Bo, Mina and Raj, must finish a class task within 21 days: a wall chart and a 6-min oral talk on a topic from an instructor. An instructor has put out a rubric and a list of original works. Start from that actual task. This plan cannot supply its topic or add fictional official grading policy.

Study our task as a group

At a first group discussion, study your rubric along with task instructions. Find all compulsory outputs. Log a final cutoff, submission path, format constraints and citation instructions. If anything is confusing, ask your instructor promptly. A group's assumption cannot turn into an official obligation.

Build a common task list from your rubric. Mark compulsory work apart from optional ambitions. A fancy wall chart can still miss a task's point. A long talk can contain good study and still surpass 6 min. Both outputs call for planning; doing a talk cannot automatically finish a wall chart.

Plan how all four will stay in contact, find common drafts and join discussions. Work with classroom tools you hold. A common digital draft can work, as can a physical portfolio and log. What counts is that all four can find a matching working draft without asking its author to hunt for it.

Split work fairly

Four matching chunks do not automatically imply fair workloads. Auditing claims, drawing a chart, drafting captions and practising a talk call for distinct amounts of work. Ask all pupils about availability, skills and tasks worth practising. For any task, assign a first author and an additional pal for an audit.

Ali might map claims to original works, Bo might draft a wall chart's layout, Mina might build a talk plan, and Raj might track work and submission tasks. Such jobs link work; all four still draft claims, audit a pal's contribution and drill oral parts. A log is important work, but it cannot act as a justification for avoiding all additional contributions.

Clarify what counts as a task fit for submission. "Study our topic" is too broad. "Draft two claims with a citation location for both, and ask Bo for an audit by day 5" is fit for an audit. Adapt this illustration to actual instructions and availability. Assign jobs prior to a final cutoff turning into a crisis.

Days 1 to 7: study and plan

During days 1 and 2, study instructions, assign jobs and start a log. During days 3 to 5, study original works in your instructor's list and draft a small body of claims with support. On day 6, discuss conflicting findings. On day 7, fix a main point for both wall chart and talk.

Aim for a full plan, a list linking claims to citations and rough allocations for oral parts. Such goals mark your own plan; consult your rubric for actual marking policy. If original works call for additional study, find that out now, not during final artwork.

Audit claims against original works

For all factual claims, log which original work supports a claim and a location: part, paragraph, diagram or similar signpost. Study surrounding paragraphs too. A short lookup summary or a pal's account cannot stand for studying original works. Ask if it supports your wording, limits and claims with counts.

Distinguish quotations, paraphrasing and your own conclusions. Mark quotations faithfully and follow your instructor's citation policy. For paraphrasing, draft from your grasp of a claim, and audit against its original wording. Swapping a handful of words is not a sound shortcut. Do not add a fictional citation just to support a claim that sounds convincing.

If Ali and Bo clash on a claim, first put it in writing. Both study a matching part of an original work and say how it supports a claim. It might justify only a claim with additional limits. Modify your draft accordingly, mark doubt if fitting, or omit a claim that cannot gain support within this task.

A factual conflict cannot vanish through a majority poll. If original works conflict or a rubric is ambiguous, log that doubt and ask your instructor about that conflict, citing both parts. Carry on with distinct tasks that do not call for that input. A final draft must not pass off claims still in doubt as facts.

A common work log

Log task, author, output, cutoff, status, auditing pal and following action. Show work without ranking a pupil's worth. A fictional illustration follows:

Day | Task | Author | Output | Status | Audit | Following action
3 | Support claim A | Ali | Claim plus location in Work A | Draft | Bo | Audit original part
5 | Wall chart plan | Bo | Layout and caption slots | Draft | Mina | Match rubric
8 | Talk plan | Mina | Four oral parts with transitions | Draft | Raj | Try talk with a clock
10 | Submission audit | Raj | Cutoff and format from task | Draft | Ali | Confirm instructions

Work A and claim A stand for actual input works; this log contains no actual study findings. Put actual citations in your own log. Log days if known. If a task slips, log its actual status and a following action. Do not mark missing work as final. A log can support planning only if it mirrors actual work.

Days 8 to 14: build and unify

On days 8 and 9, build a wall chart and talk from your common plan. On days 10 and 11, audit claims and citations. On day 12, unify writing. On days 13 and 14, try a full talk with a clock and modify its plan if it runs long.

Contributors might pick distinct words for a common point, add matching introductions or skip background. Fix a common vocabulary and uniform diagram tags. Study a full draft from start to finish, not just your own part. Hold important distinctions from original works; uniform writing cannot justify distorting a claim.

A wall chart should stand on its own. Add a main point that stands out, a logical layout and captions clarifying what a diagram adds. Your actual rubric controls what to put in. An oral talk can walk a class through important points without saying all wall-chart words aloud.

A 6-min oral plan

A 6-min talk lasts 360 s. Plan 90 s for Ali, 90 s for Bo, 90 s for Mina and 90 s for Raj: 90 + 90 + 90 + 90 = 360. Count introductions, transitions and a final closing within such slots. Do not add such parts on top and still claim a 6-min total.

Ali might put an initial 90 s toward your task's focus and a first point with support. Bo has 90 s for an additional point; Mina has 90 s for an additional part of your main point; Raj has a final 90 s for summing up and closing. This is a timing illustration, not a fictional account of your topic from your instructor. Adapt its main point to your actual rubric.

Drill with a clock. If a part runs 120 s, do not push a following pupil to rush just to mask it. Cut duplication, simplify wording and try again. An allocation is a plan, not proof that a final talk fits. Ask if a class discussion counts within your limit if your actual instructions do not say.

Oral comfort and missing work

A bold pupil should not claim all oral parts. A shy pupil might gain from a compact part, an initial trial with a pal and prompt cards if class policy allows. Ask what support works. Do not jump from oral discomfort to claims of a lack of motivation. Drill transitions so all pupils know both a prior pupil's last paragraph and how to start a following part.

Discuss a missing draft away from your class and focus on outputs: "Our plan has your draft down for today, and our citation audit calls for it. What is blocking you? What could you finish by tomorrow, and which parts should shift?" Do not claim you know why a pal is missing work. Aim for a sound plan that can actually work.

If a task shifts, log its author, limits and cutoff. Confirm that a pupil taking on additional work has capacity. Ongoing missing work might call for your instructor's support within actual class policy. Do not add fictional sanctions or omit contributions from a log to mask unfair workloads. Hold a faithful log and ask how to act if stuck.

Days 15 to 21: drill, audit and submit

During days 15 and 16, drill full talks, including pointing to a wall chart and handoffs. On day 17, audit timing and claims. On days 18 and 19, audit citations, formatting and submission instructions. Aim to finish prior to an official cutoff, with days 20 and 21 absorbing ordinary faults.

Stop optional additions if work fulfills your actual task and a talk flows within its limit. A last-day additional point can call for hasty modifications across your chart, citations and timing. Fix flaws and missing compulsory parts. Put optional proposals on a list for following tasks. Log a final copy all four can find and who will submit it.

Plan for a missing pal on talk day. All pupils should know surrounding parts and hold a common plan. If Bo is out, split Bo's 90 s among Ali and Mina: Ali 135, Mina 135 and Raj 90 still total 360. Drill that handoff and consult your instructor about actual class policy for a missing pupil.

A fallback supports oral flow; only actual class policy controls marks. If your instructor adjusts what class policy allows, follow that input. Hold your wall chart and supporting drafts in a common portfolio or location. A missing laptop or portfolio should not strand your group.

Finally, submit through your actual submission path, confirm submission and hold a copy. Aim for a wall chart with support for its claims and a joint talk that fits its cutoff, with a faithful log of contributions. A fancy-looking output cannot stand in for such foundations.

prompt: Write a connected practical guide for four fictional students producing a one-page school bulletin every month with teacher supervision. The page has room for three short articles, an announcement box, and one original drawing. Explain choosing an audience and purpose, gathering accurate information, assigning roles, drafting, editing for clarity, checking names and dates, arranging the page, obtaining the teacher's final review, and distributing the approved page. Include a concrete four-week production schedule, a sample article brief, a compact editing checklist, and a small mock page outline. Cover a late article, two students wanting the same role, an incorrect date caught after distribution, and a student who wants to contribute without being named. Do not invent school policy or give legal advice. Write 2,048 to 2,560 Qwen tokens of substantive useful guidance.
response:
A small school journal should do a plain job: allow pupils to find out what was, what is coming, and how to join in. Four pupils can do this on 1 folio if all opt for a small goal and work with a tutor throughout. Final approval should not act as a last-instant shock.

First ask who will look at it. For your class, familiar pupils and rooms might allow a short account. A journal for all pupils may call for additional information. Ask your tutor how a final copy can go out. Do not add a school policy or act as if all pupils can go to a particular chat without asking.

Hold your format in sight: 3 short accounts, a box for what's on, and an original drawing. All must fit 1 folio. An additional account must push a part out, not turn 1 folio into 2 without discussion. Pick parts that aid pupils, not just anything that will fill a gap.

A goal could say: "Our monthly journal shows 3 parts of school days and aids pupils in finding club tasks." This can inform a pick if 2 parts want a spot. A part might fit a following month, though it sounds good now. All four should say what fits; a bold pupil should not hold all authority.

A 4-part monthly plan

Days1-7: pick accounts, list facts to find out, and assign jobs.
Days8-14: find information, draft all 3 accounts, and plan a drawing.
Days15-21: trim, audit who/which day/what hour, and build a full copy.
Days22-28: obtain tutor approval, fix flaws, hand out prints, and log what should shift.

Do not put a final audit at distribution's actual instant. Allow a gap for your tutor to look and for pupils to act on that input. Work backward from your distribution day. Ask how long a tutor wants to do an audit, not how long you wish it would last.

A fictional job split could put Ali on planning accounts, Boris on auditing facts, Mina on art and layout, and Noor on draft tracking and distribution. A job is not a claim to block input. Our fictional school plot spans 6 cm by 4 cm on a map. Its map ratio is 1 cm to 5 m. Thus a 1 cm span on this drawing stands for a 5 m span on actual ground. Our map is a small diagram of school land, not an additional plot.

A full lap follows all four boundary parts. Two long parts supply 30 + 30 m. Two short parts supply 20 + 20 m. Add all parts: 30 + 20 + 30 + 20 = 100 m. This counts a walk around our plot, not how much land it holds.

For its footprint, multiply actual spans: 30 m x 20 m = 600 m^2. A 1 m by 1 m box holds 1 m^2 of land. Our plot holds 600 such box units. A lap calls for m; a footprint calls for m^2. Such units quantify distinct things, so writing 600 m for a footprint would fail.

Think of a railing and a crop. A railing follows our plot's boundary, so a full railing without gaps calls for 100 m. A crop grows on our plot, so its footprint is 600 m^2. On our map, a footprint is 6 cm x 4 cm = 24 cm^2. Draw a grid with columns 1 cm across and rows 1 cm high. Six columns and four rows contain 24 small box units. Any box is 1 cm by 1 cm on our map.

Our map ratio works across both width and long span. Thus a small map box stands for an actual patch 5 m by 5 m. Its footprint is 5 x 5 = 25 m^2, not just 5 m^2. Multiplying along only a width would form a long strip, not a fully grown patch.

Watch units in this claim. Our ratio is 1 cm to 5 m. That is not a factor of 5 across matching units. Put both spans in cm to obtain 1 cm to 500 cm, a ratio of 1:500. prompt: Explain fair division through a fictional classroom with 24 identical art tokens and four groups named Ash, Birch, Fir, and Oak. Begin with an equal split. Then suppose the groups contain 2, 3, 3, and 4 students respectively and explain a proportional split by student count. Next suppose each group must receive at least 2 tokens before the remaining tokens are allocated proportionally by group size; show the exact fractional shares, explain why whole tokens cause a rounding issue, and demonstrate one transparent allocation rule. Discuss how different fairness rules answer different questions, how to state a rule before seeing who benefits, and how to handle a tie in remainders. Include a complete arithmetic check, a short fictional disagreement with respectful resolution, and two practice variations with worked answers. These are toy classroom rules, not universal moral conclusions. Write 2,048 to 2,560 Qwen tokens of substantive explanation.
response:
An art class has 24 matching chips. A chip funds a small art supply. Four groups, Ash, Birch, Fir and Oak, must split this stock. For this task, no chip can turn into parts. A fractional allocation can quantify a math goal, but an actual handout must consist of intact chips.

Calling a split fair cannot fully fix a calculation. Fair to groups, fair to individual pupils, and fair to groups with a minimum supply can imply distinct allocations. First clarify what a policy aims to accomplish. Our fictional classroom can show how such plans work without justifying moral conclusions for all situations.

A uniform start

All four groups gain a matching count. Split 24 into 4 parts to obtain 6. Ash has 6, Birch has 6, Fir has 6, and Oak has 6. Our audit is 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24.

This policy counts a group as its unit. It might fit a task in which all groups build murals of matching form. It cannot also imply a matching supply for all pupils. That distinction is important if group populations vary.

Now Ash has 2 pupils, Birch has 3, Fir has 3, and Oak has 4. Our total is 2 + 3 + 3 + 4 = 12 pupils. With uniform group allocations, Ash has 6/2 = 3 chips for a pupil; Birch and Fir both hold 6/3 = 2; Oak holds 6/4 = 1.5. Such ratios quantify a group's stock, not an instruction to cut chips in half.

A proportional split

If our aim is a uniform allocation for all pupils, split 24 chips among 12 pupils. This grants 2 chips to a pupil. Multiply all group populations by 2:

Ash: 2 x 2 = 4
Birch: 3 x 2 = 6
Fir: 3 x 2 = 6
Oak: 4 x 2 = 8

Our total is 4 + 6 + 6 + 8 = 24. Individual ratios stand at 4/2 = 2, 6/3 = 2, 6/3 = 2 and 8/4 = 2. All groups now hold matching ratios of chips to pupils. Group totals vary with pupil counts.

Both calculations work. A uniform split fits a task about matching group totals. A proportional split fits a task about matching individual ratios. A conflict among participants might focus on goals, not on faulty division.

A minimum, plus a proportional addition

Now our class wants all groups to hold a minimum of 2 chips for a common starting task. Following that initial allocation, split all additional chips proportionally by pupil count. This policy joins a group minimum with additional supply following individual counts.

First put away 4 x 2 = 8 chips. Of our original stock, 24 - 8 = 16 still await allocation. Splitting 16 among 12 pupils grants 16/12 = 4/3 additional chips for a pupil. Add a minimum of 2 to all proportional group additions:

Ash: 2 + 2 x 4/3 = 2 + 8/3 = 14/3.
Birch: 2 + 3 x 4/3 = 2 + 4 = 6.
Fir: 2 + 3 x 4/3 = 6.
Oak: 2 + 4 x 4/3 = 2 + 16/3 = 22/3.

Audit our total without rounding: 14/3 + 6 + 6 + 22/3 = 36/3 + 12 = 24. All four allocations surpass our minimum of 2. Our additions, prior to adding that minimum, follow a ratio of 2:3:3:4, as our policy calls for.

This cannot supply uniform final ratios for all pupils. Ash's ratio is (14/3)/2 = 7/3, but Oak's is (22/3)/4 = 11/6. A common group minimum has additional impact for a pupil in a small group. That is part of our policy, not a flaw in its math.

Making an actual handout

Our class cannot actually hand Ash 14/3 intact chips. A policy for rounding can first round all fractional group allocations down, and hand out any additional chips by ranking fractional parts from high to low. This is a valid policy; our task cannot show that it is obligatory.

Our downward allocations stand at 4, 6, 6 and 7. That sums to 23, so 1 chip still awaits allocation. Find fractional parts:

Ash: 14/3 - 4 = 2/3.
Birch: 6 - 6 = 0.
Fir: 6 - 6 = 0.
Oak: 22/3 - 7 = 1/3.

Ash's fractional part is maximum, so Ash gains our final chip. Our actual handout is 5, 6, 6 and 7. Audit 5 + 6 + 6 + 7 = 24. Confirm that all groups still hold a minimum of 2. Ash's 5 tops its fractional allocation by 1/3; Oak's 7 falls short by 1/3. Birch and Fir match fully.

Rounding 14/3 to 5 and 22/3 to 7 works on this input, but rounding fractions individually cannot always maintain a total stock. A policy must account for all chips. Downward rounding puts our initial sum at most at our stock, and our following actions hand out all that still awaits allocation. No chip is lost, nor can a chip spring from nothing.

Choosing plans and handling draws

Put a policy in writing prior to finding out which group gains from it. Clarify stock, units, minimums, formulas, rounding, and a policy for draws in fractional parts. Without this prior pact, a participant might pick a policy simply to award that participant's own group additional chips.

For a draw, a straightforward classroom custom is A-to-Z ranking of group tags. If Birch and Fir hold matching fractional parts and only a solitary chip still awaits allocation, Birch wins. This custom is straightforward to audit, but group tags carry no intrinsic claim to priority. Using it across many rounds might always favor a particular group.

A class could opt for a public random draw among groups with matching fractional parts, or a rotation log that shifts priority round by round. Fix that policy first, including how to act if a draw occurs again. Do not switch plans on finding out who wins. For our following trials, stick to A-to-Z ranking throughout.

A short conflict

Ali said, "Ash is small, but our common mural is as big as Oak's. Why should our basic supply fall short?"

Omar said, "Oak has four pupils doing individual art. With six chips for both groups, our pupils hold only half as much individually as yours."

Mina had both clarify goals without insults. Ali sought a minimum supply for a group task. Omar sought additional supply following pupil count. Both saw that 24 chips could not fund all wants.

For a forthcoming activity, all said that a minimum-plus-proportional policy would fit. Mina put its rounding policy and its draw custom in writing prior to assigning pupils to groups for that activity. For our illustration, all found 5, 6, 6 and 7 from our input counts. Mina said, "All of us now know this input. Our illustration cannot show that our policy was put into writing without knowing who would gain."

Ali saw that a common start did not imply matching final group totals. Omar saw that a group minimum would shift individual ratios. All did an audit of our math and put both a final plan and its limits on a chalkboard. A pact could follow without claiming that all goals now fully align.

Two trials

Trial 1: Hold populations at 2, 3, 3 and 4, but put out 30 chips and no minimum. What proportional allocation of intact chips follows our rounding policy?

Our class still has 12 pupils. A fractional allocation for a pupil is 30/12 = 5/2 chips. Group allocations prior to rounding stand at 5, 15/2, 15/2 and 10. Our sum is 30. Round down to 5, 7, 7 and 10, totaling 29. Birch and Fir draw with fractional parts of 1/2; Ash and Oak both hold fractional parts of 0.

Only a solitary chip still awaits allocation. Our A-to-Z pact awards it to Birch. Our actual split is 5, 8, 7 and 10, which sums to 30. Birch and Fir hold matching populations and matching fractional allocations, but intact chips cannot supply a half chip to both. Our custom sorts out that practical draw, but a winning draw is not a moral proof.

Trial 2: Start with 12 chips, hold our original populations, and insist on a minimum of 2 for all groups prior to splitting additional chips proportionally. What fractional allocations and actual handout follow?

Put away 8 chips, so 4 still await allocation. Our proportional addition for a pupil is 4/12 = 1/3. Group totals now stand at 2 + 2/3 = 8/3, 2 + 1 = 3, 3, and 2 + 4/3 = 10/3. Our sum is 18/3 + 6 = 12.

Round down to 2, 3, 3 and 3, totaling 11. Ash has a fractional part of 2/3, Oak has 1/3, and both additional groups hold 0. Ash gains our final chip, producing 3, 3, 3 and 3. Matching totals follow from this particular input and rounding policy. Our minimum-plus-proportional policy cannot always imply uniform group totals.

Finally, audit a minimum for viability prior to starting any calculation. A stock of only 7 chips cannot fund four minimums of 2, as that calls for 8. In that situation our class must shift its stock or its pact and say why. No form of rounding can fund a minimum surpassing our total stock.
